consensus_summary: Faith centrally means confident, trusting reliance on God and, in Christian teaching, on Christ for salvation; living faith is associated with obedience and works, while faithfulness or allegiance is a recognized secondary nuance.
book_summary: Faith is “trusting faithfulness”: persevering reliance on God’s unseen promise that expresses itself in obedience. Works neither earn the promise nor replace faith, but enact faith and bring it to maturity; workless faith is dead.
rationale: The entry retains the consensus core of reliance on God and his promises but more tightly integrates fidelity, obedience, and James’s account of faith being perfected through works. This emphasis is represented in the blind responses, so it is neither divergent nor novel, but it materially sharpens the common formulation of faith as the sole instrument of justification.
strongest_objection: The formulation may blur the distinction between faith itself and the works that evidence or complete it, whereas many mainstream Protestant accounts define justifying faith as trust alone and treat obedience strictly as its necessary fruit. The entry partly answers this by explicitly denying that works purchase the promise.
